Use the keyboard home row and essential keys.
Log in safely and choose sleep or shut down.

topics.title: Typing and Keyboard Shortcuts
topics.summary: This topic builds confident typing habits and introduces the most useful keyboard shortcuts. You will learn correct posture, practice accuracy, and use shortcuts that save time in every subject.
learningGoals: Sit and type with safe, comfortable posture.
Use the home row and build muscle memory.
Use core shortcuts for copy, paste, save, select all, and undo.
Take and manage screenshots.
Understand the clipboard and undo.

lessons.title: Touch Typing Posture and Home Row

keywords.definition: Typing without looking at the keys.
The middle row of keys (ASDF JKL;).
How you sit and hold your body while working.

coreContent: Good posture helps you type comfortably and avoid pain. Sit with your feet flat on the floor and your back straight. Keep your elbows about 90 degrees and your wrists level, not bent up or down. The top of the screen should be around eye level. Place your fingers on the home row. Use the bumps on F and J to find the correct position. Your thumbs rest on the space bar. This position helps your fingers learn where keys are without looking.
keyReminders: Do not rest your wrists on the desk edge.
Short practice every day is better than one long session.
tryIt: Sit correctly and place your fingers on ASDF JKL;.
Type the home row letters slowly and correctly.
quickCheck: What are the home row keys?
Why do F and J have bumps?
What should your wrists look like while typing?
lessons.didYouKnow: Professional typists can average 75 words per minute with high accuracy.
commonPitfalls: Looking at the keys instead of the screen.
Slouching or bending wrists.
lessons.examTip: The home row keys are ASDF JKL;.

lessons.title: Building Typing Speed and Accuracy

keywords.definition: Your fingers learning positions through practice.

coreContent: Accuracy comes first. When you type the right letters, your speed will improve naturally. Practice short phrases, your name, and simple sentences. Use a typing test tool to track words per minute (WPM) and accuracy. Correct mistakes as soon as you see them. This builds good habits and stops errors from becoming permanent.
keyReminders: Slow and accurate is better than fast and messy.
Practice for 10 minutes a day to improve.
tryIt: Take a 1 minute typing test and write down your accuracy.
Practice the same sentence twice and try to reduce mistakes.
quickCheck: Why should you focus on accuracy first?
What does WPM mean?
How long should a daily practice session be?
lessons.didYouKnow: The world record for typing speed is over 200 words per minute.
commonPitfalls: Rushing and making lots of errors.
Ignoring mistakes instead of fixing them.
lessons.examTip: Accuracy builds correct muscle memory.

lessons.title: Core Keyboard Shortcuts

keywords.definition: A key combination that does a task quickly.
Duplicate selected text or a file.
Place copied text or a file.
The main shortcut key on a Mac (Cmd).

coreContent: Shortcuts save time in every subject. Hold the Command key and tap the letter key: - Cmd+C = Copy - Cmd+V = Paste - Cmd+S = Save - Cmd+A = Select all - Cmd+Z = Undo To use a shortcut, keep Command pressed, tap the other key, then release both.
keyReminders: Memorize these five shortcuts.
Practice in any text box.
tryIt: Type a sentence, highlight it, and use Cmd+C then Cmd+V.
Save your work with Cmd+S.
quickCheck: What does Cmd+S do?
Which shortcut selects all text?
How do you undo a mistake?
lessons.didYouKnow: The Command symbol comes from Scandinavian road signs.
commonPitfalls: Letting go of Command too early.
Using the mouse for everything instead of shortcuts.
lessons.examTip: Cmd+S means Save.

lessons.title: Screenshot Techniques

keywords.definition: The main screen area where files can appear.

coreContent: Use Cmd+Shift+3 to capture the whole screen. Use Cmd+Shift+4 to capture a selected area. Your cursor becomes a crosshair; drag to select the area. Screenshots save to the Desktop by default. Rename screenshots and move them into a folder so your Desktop stays clean. Press Esc to cancel a screenshot.
keyReminders: The crosshair means you are selecting an area.
Delete old screenshots you do not need.
tryIt: Take a full screen screenshot.
Take a small area screenshot and rename the file.
quickCheck: Which shortcut captures the whole screen?

lessons.title: Clipboard and Undo Operations

keywords.definition: Temporary storage for one copied item.

coreContent: When you copy something, it goes to the clipboard. The clipboard holds one item at a time. If you copy a new item, the old one is replaced. Use Cmd+Z to undo mistakes in most apps. Use Cmd+Shift+Z to redo. Undo is a safe way to fix errors without deleting lots of work.
keyReminders: Paste before you copy something new.
Undo works in almost every app.
tryIt: Copy a word, paste it, then copy a new word and paste again.
Make a mistake and use Cmd+Z to fix it.
quickCheck: How many items can the clipboard hold?
What does Cmd+Z do?

lessons.didYouKnow: The idea of a clipboard was first used in early computers in the 1970s.
commonPitfalls: Thinking the clipboard saves many items.

coreContent: You can create your own shortcuts and text replacements in System Settings under Keyboard. For example, you can set "omw" to become "On my way". These settings work across most apps. topics.title: Finder and File Management
topics.summary: This topic shows you how to find, organize, and manage files. You will use Finder, follow the OneDrive rule, and keep your folders tidy.
learningGoals: Use Finder to locate files and folders.
Save work in OneDrive and check sync status.
Create folders with clear names and structure.
Move, copy, search, and delete files safely.

lessons.title: Understanding Finder and the Desktop

keywords.definition: The app that helps you find files and folders.
The main screen area where icons appear.
The row of app icons at the bottom of the screen.
The bar at the top that changes for each app.

coreContent: Finder is the file browser on a Mac. It is the blue smiley face icon in the Dock. Use Finder to open folders, move files, and search for work. The Desktop is a workspace, not a storage place. Use it for temporary files only, then move them into folders. The menu bar changes based on the app you are using. The Dock helps you open apps and see which ones are running.
keyReminders: Keep the Desktop clean.
Check the menu bar to see which app is active.
tryIt: Open Finder and look at the sidebar, toolbar, and search bar.
Move one file from the Desktop into a folder.
quickCheck: What is Finder used for?
Why should the Desktop stay clean?
Where do you find the menu bar?
lessons.didYouKnow: Finder has been part of macOS since 1984.
commonPitfalls: Using the Desktop as permanent storage.
Looking for app settings in the wrong menu bar.

lessons.title: The OneDrive Rule and Cloud Storage

keywords.definition: Files stored online and synced to devices.
When files update between your MacBook and the cloud.
Files stored only on your MacBook.

coreContent: The OneDrive rule is simple: save everything to OneDrive. Cloud storage keeps your work safe and available on any device. Local storage ("On My Mac") is not backed up. Look for status icons. A green check means the file is synced. Spinning arrows mean syncing. A red X means an error. If you see a red X, tell your teacher.
keyReminders: Check for a green check before closing your MacBook.
Use OneDrive for all school files.
tryIt: Save a document to your OneDrive folder.

quickCheck: Why should you save to OneDrive?

lessons.didYouKnow: Your files are stored in secure data centers and can be opened on any device with your school login.
commonPitfalls: Saving work to "On My Mac" instead of OneDrive.

lessons.title: Creating and Naming Folders

keywords.definition: A clear, consistent way to name files and folders.
A folder structure with levels (Year, Subject, Topic).

coreContent: Create a new folder by right clicking (two-finger tap) and choosing New Folder. Name it immediately. Use clear names like "English_Essay" or "Science_Projects". Avoid special characters like / \ : * ? " < > | because they break file paths. Build a simple hierarchy: Year7 > Subject > Topic. This makes it easy to find your work later.
keyReminders: Name folders right away.
Keep names short, clear, and consistent.
tryIt: Create a Year7 folder, then add two subject folders.
Rename a folder by clicking its name once, then again.
quickCheck: Which characters should you avoid in file names?

How do you rename a folder?
lessons.didYouKnow: The folder icon is based on a real paper folder used in offices.
commonPitfalls: Leaving folders named "Untitled".
Using symbols that break file names.
lessons.examTip: A valid name uses letters, numbers, and underscores.

lessons.title: File Operations and Navigation

keywords.definition: Two quick clicks to open a file or folder.
Click and move a file to a new place.
Find files by typing in the Finder search bar.
Preview a file by pressing the space bar.

Quick Look lets you preview a file without opening it. Press the space bar to open Quick Look, then press it again to close. Use the Finder search bar to find files quickly.

Quick Look saves time.

lessons.title: Trash and File Deletion

keywords.definition: The place where deleted files go first.
Files are gone and cannot be recovered easily.

coreContent: To delete a file, drag it to the Trash or press Cmd+Delete. The file stays in the Trash until you empty it. You can restore files from the Trash before emptying. Empty the Trash to free storage space. Always check the Trash before you empty it to avoid deleting important work.
keyReminders: Trash is not permanent until you empty it.
Check before you empty the Trash.
tryIt: Move a test file to the Trash, then restore it.

lessons.didYouKnow: Files in the Trash still use storage space.
commonPitfalls: Forgetting to empty the Trash.

topics.title: Apps and Window Control
topics.summary: This topic shows you how to open apps, control windows, and switch between tasks. You will learn the traffic light buttons, how to quit apps, and how to use split view and multiple desktops.
learningGoals: Open apps using the Dock, Launchpad, and Spotlight.
Use the window control buttons correctly.
Quit apps when you are finished.
Switch between apps and manage multiple windows.
Use full screen, split view, and multiple desktops.

lessons.title: Opening Applications (Dock, Launchpad, Spotlight)

keywords.definition: The row of app icons at the bottom of the screen.
A grid that shows all apps.
A search tool that opens apps quickly.
A program you use on your MacBook.

coreContent: The Dock shows your most used apps. Click an icon to open the app. A small dot under the icon means the app is running. Launchpad shows every app on your MacBook. Open it with the Launchpad key (F4 on some keyboards) or a pinch with thumb and three fingers on the trackpad. Spotlight is the fastest way to open any app. Press Cmd+Space, type the app name, then press Return.
keyReminders: Use Spotlight for apps that are not in the Dock.
The dot under an icon means the app is open.
tryIt: Open Word using the Dock.
Open OneNote using Spotlight.
quickCheck: Which tool shows all apps in a grid?
What shortcut opens Spotlight?

lessons.didYouKnow: Spotlight can also do quick calculations and conversions.
commonPitfalls: Searching for apps in Finder instead of Spotlight.
lessons.examTip: Cmd+Space opens Spotlight.

lessons.title: Window Control Buttons (Traffic Lights)

keywords.definition: The red, yellow, and green buttons on a window.
Yellow button, hides the window in the Dock.
Green button, makes the window fill the screen.

coreContent: Every window has three buttons in the top left corner. Red closes the window. Yellow minimizes it to the Dock. Green makes the window full screen. Closing a window does not always quit the app. If the app is still running, you will see a dot under its icon in the Dock.
keyReminders: Red closes a window, not the app.
Full screen hides the menu bar; move the cursor to the top to see it.
tryIt: Open a window and try each button.

lessons.title: Quitting vs Closing Applications

keywords.definition: A small mark under a Dock icon that shows an app is running.

coreContent: Closing a window only hides it. The app can still run in the background. To fully close an app, use Cmd+Q or right click the Dock icon and choose Quit. Quitting apps you are not using saves memory and helps your MacBook run smoothly.

coreContent: Use Cmd+Tab to switch between open apps. Hold Cmd and tap Tab to move through the list. Use Cmd+Shift+Tab to move backward. Mission Control shows all open windows. Use a three-finger swipe up on the trackpad to open it. The menu bar always shows the active app.

topics.title: Word and PowerPoint Essentials
topics.summary: This topic helps you choose the right Office app and use it well. You will learn Word and PowerPoint basics, clear formatting, saving with AutoSave, and sharing work with teachers.
learningGoals: Choose Word or PowerPoint for the task.
Format text clearly in Word.
Create and organize slides in PowerPoint.

lessons.title: Email vs Teams - When to Use Each
coreContent: Use email for formal messages, especially when writing to teachers. Email is good for longer messages, attachments, and official requests. Use Teams for quick questions, class chats, and group work. If you need a record of a request or you are sending work, email is usually best.

Use Teams for quick class messages.

units.overview: This unit helps you feel confident using your school MacBook and the main apps we use at St George's. You will learn how to handle the device safely, organize your files, and work in Word, PowerPoint, OneDrive, Teams, and OneNote. The goal is strong habits that make every future unit easier.
objectives: Navigate the macOS interface (Finder, Dock, Launchpad, menu bar, file paths).
Create and maintain an organized folder structure for schoolwork.
Save, locate, and manage files using OneDrive and local storage.
Use Teams as the hub for messages, assignments, and resources.
Use OneNote Class Notebook (Content Library and personal section).
Understand the difference between local and cloud storage.
Work safely and respectfully in shared digital spaces.

concepts.name: Adaptation
concepts.description: How people and systems adjust to new tools and workflows. In this unit: you adapt to the school's digital ecosystem and build new routines.

concepts.name: Form
concepts.description: How information is organized and structured. In this unit: you build clear folder structures and use sections and pages in OneNote.

concepts.name: Function
concepts.description: The purpose of tools and systems. In this unit: you learn why we use Teams, OneDrive, and OneNote.

skills: Digital Literacy: using devices, apps, and settings safely.
Data Handling: saving, naming, and organizing files.
Creativity in Technology: choosing the right tool to present ideas.
howToUse: Read the keywords first, then the core content.
Try the Quick check questions after each lesson.
Use the Common pitfalls to avoid mistakes.
If English is new to you, underline new words and ask your teacher for support.
quickStart: Charge your MacBook and bring it to every lesson.
Ask a teacher if you are unsure about a setting.

whatYouLearned: Physical skills: Safe handling of the MacBook, trackpad gestures, keyboard basics, and power management.
File management: The OneDrive rule, folder structures, naming, and safe deletion.
Application skills: Opening apps, managing windows, and choosing Word or PowerPoint.
Communication: Writing clear emails and knowing when to use Teams or email.
Organization: Using OneNote sections, tags, and sync status.
keyHabits: Always save to OneDrive, not On My Mac.
Check sync status before closing OneNote or your MacBook.
Use clear file and folder names.
Use core shortcuts: Cmd+C, Cmd+V, Cmd+S, Cmd+Shift+3, Cmd+Z.
Keep your Desktop and inbox tidy.
summary.lookingAhead: These digital habits will support every future Computer Science unit. The more automatic they become, the more time you have for creative and challenging tasks.
revisionChecklist: I can find files in Finder and use Search.
I can explain the difference between Sleep and Shut Down.
I can use the five core shortcuts without looking.
I save all work to OneDrive and check for the green check.
I can write a clear email with a subject, greeting, and closing.
I know the five OneNote sections and where to find homework.
I know when to use Word vs PowerPoint.
I can quit apps properly and use Split View.
finalExamTips: Review the Common pitfalls in each lesson.
Memorize the Keywords for each topic.
Practice the interactive activities to build muscle memory.
Ask your teacher if any step is still unclear.
